why.support: Getting around means reading **maps** and **apps**, and asking for directions. Get it right, and you can get anywhere.
why.core: Getting around is a reading and speaking job. You read **maps**, **symbols** and **apps**. You ask for directions and check you've understood them. And you give directions other people can actually follow. Get it right, and you can get yourself anywhere: to work, to TAFE, to a gig and home again.
why.extend: Navigating a transport network means reading multimodal texts (maps, symbols, apps and alerts) and using spoken interaction to gather and confirm information. Each text makes choices about what to show and what to leave out, so knowing how they work makes you a more independent traveller.

articles.title: How to get around

body.support:
Since **1 January 2026**, anyone in Victoria under 18 can catch trains, trams and buses for **free** with a **Youth myki**. Here's how to get where you're going.

**1. Read the map.** Find the **map key**. It tells you what the colours and **symbols** mean. Look for **interchanges**: places where you can change lines.

**2. Use a journey planner app.** Type where you're going. Choose **leave at** or **arrive by**. Check for **disruptions**.

**3. Check the front.** The train or bus shows where it's going.

**4. Have a Plan B.** Charge your phone. Know when the last service leaves.

**5. Ask, and say it back.** *So I turn left, then it's next to the shop?*

**6. Give clear directions.** Say the steps in order. Use **landmarks**, like a big church.
body.core:
Since **1 January 2026**, anyone in Victoria under 18 can catch trains, trams and buses for **free** with a **Youth myki**. It costs $5 to buy, and you still tap on and off. Free travel only helps if you can work out where you're going. Here's how.

**1. Read the map.** Start with the **map key**. It explains what each colour, line and **symbol** means. Look for **interchanges**, where lines meet and you can change. Most train maps are **diagrams**: they straighten the lines and space out the stations so they're easier to read. That means they don't show real distances.

**2. Use a journey planner.** Apps like the PTV app or Google Maps plan your trip for you. Type where you're going, then choose **leave at** or **arrive by**. Check the platform, the stop and the time to **change**. Always check **alerts** for **disruptions**: if trains aren't running, there may be a **replacement bus**.

**3. Check the destination.** Trains and buses show where they're going on the front. Make sure it's the right one, in the right direction.

**4. Have a Plan B.** Charge your phone. Know when the last service home leaves. Save a number to call if you get stuck.

**5. Ask for directions, and check them.** Station staff are there to help. When someone gives you directions, **paraphrase** them back: *So I go out the main exit, turn left, and it's next to the post office?*

**6. Give directions people can follow.** Start with where they are. Give the steps **in order**. Use **landmarks** they can see, like a big church or a bridge. And tell them how they'll know they've gone too far.
body.extend:
Since **1 January 2026**, all Victorians under 18 can travel free on trains, trams and buses with a **Youth myki** ($5, with tap-on and tap-off still required). Using the network well depends on reading its texts.

**1. Read the map.** The **map key** (or legend) explains colours, lines and **symbols**. **Interchanges** show where routes connect. Network maps are usually **diagrams**, not to scale: lines are straightened and stations evenly spaced. This makes the map easier to read, but it hides real distances and geography. Every map is a set of choices about what to show.

**2. Use a journey planner.** Apps such as the PTV app or Google Maps calculate routes. Set **leave at** or **arrive by**, then check platforms, stops and connection times. Real-time **alerts** flag **disruptions** and **replacement buses**.

**3. Confirm the destination** shown on the vehicle and the direction of travel.

**4. Plan for failure.** Battery, data and last services are all points of failure. Know the last service home and a backup.

**5. Clarify spoken directions.** **Paraphrase** them back and ask questions: *So I take the main exit, turn left, and it's opposite the bakery?*

**6. Give directions with a clear structure:** a starting point, sequenced steps, visible **landmarks**, and a check (*if you reach the bridge, you've gone too far*).

caseStudies.title: The map that changed

body.support:
Some trains in Melbourne used to go through the **City Loop**.

Then the **Metro Tunnel** opened. From **1 February 2026**, trains on the **Sunbury**, **Cranbourne** and **Pakenham** lines go through the new tunnel instead. It has **five new stations**, like **Town Hall** and **State Library**.

Lots of people had to find a new way. The advice was to **change trains** at Town Hall or State Library.

The map was redrawn. An old map could send you the wrong way. So always check the latest map or app.
body.core:
For years, people on Melbourne's **Sunbury**, **Cranbourne** and **Pakenham** lines rode their trains through the **City Loop**, past stations like Flinders Street and Melbourne Central.

Then the **Metro Tunnel** opened. Its first trains ran on **30 November 2025**. From **1 February 2026**, all trains on those three lines started running through the new tunnel **instead** of the City Loop. The tunnel has **five new underground stations**: **Arden**, **Parkville**, **State Library**, **Town Hall** and **Anzac**.

That changed how thousands of people get around. Someone who always got off at Flinders Street now had to plan a new way. The government's advice was to **change trains**:

- at **Town Hall**, and walk through the Degraves Street subway to Flinders Street, or
- at **State Library**, and walk through the underground concourse to Melbourne Central.

People from the south-east going to South Yarra, Richmond or Parliament were told to change at **Caulfield**.

The network map was redrawn. Anyone using an old map, or an old habit, could end up in the wrong place. The lesson: maps and routes change. Check the latest map, and use a journey planner, every time something's new.
body.extend:
For decades, trains on Melbourne's **Sunbury**, **Cranbourne** and **Pakenham** lines ran through the **City Loop**.

The **Metro Tunnel**'s first trains ran on **30 November 2025**. From **1 February 2026**, all trains on those lines ran through the tunnel **instead of** the City Loop. The tunnel has **five new underground stations**: **Arden**, **Parkville**, **State Library**, **Town Hall** and **Anzac**.

For thousands of regular travellers, familiar routes stopped working. The official advice named new places to change trains:

- **Town Hall**, linked by the Degraves Street subway to Flinders Street;
- **State Library**, linked by an underground concourse to Melbourne Central;
- **Caulfield**, for south-east travellers heading to South Yarra, Richmond or Parliament.

The network map was redrawn to match. The case shows that a map shows a network at one point in time. When the network changes, old maps and old habits can mislead. Checking the current map and a live journey planner is part of reading the network.

teacher.overview: Students learn to read transport maps (key, symbols, lines, interchanges) and understand that network maps are diagrams that make choices about what to show. They use journey planner apps (leave at / arrive by, alerts, disruptions) and plan a backup. The speaking focus is asking for directions and paraphrasing them back to check, and giving directions with a start point, ordered steps, landmarks and a gone-too-far check. The case study is the 2025–26 Metro Tunnel change, which redrew Melbourne's train map.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** what each colour, line and symbol means. When you need to be somewhere by a set time. Plan B: charged phone, last service time, someone to call, a backup route.

**Map key (samples):** a station or stop; an interchange; an accessible station; a different kind of service (often a bus or a line under construction, check your key); something left out: real distances, streets, hills, how long the walk between platforms is.

**Directions:** 1 start point; 2 direction and distance; 3 landmark; 4 next step in order; 5 gone-too-far check; 6 destination clue.

**Sort:** down there a bit — confusing; left at the lights — clear; can't miss it — confusing; Town Hall, Swanston St exit — clear; old servo — confusing (they can't see it); bridge check — clear.

**Case study:** trains on those lines run through the Metro Tunnel instead of the City Loop, with five new stations, so people had to change trains to reach old stops; an old map shows a network that no longer exists; check the current map or journey planner whenever something changes.

**Scenarios (samples):** follow signs to the replacement buses and allow extra time; check the app for another route or service, or call someone you saved in your Plan B; ask station staff, use a printed map, or a help point.

realityCheck: **Regional schools:** the case study is about Melbourne, but the skills aren't. Use your local bus map and V/Line timetable for the activities.
**Some students rarely travel alone.** For them, the Do it is the most valuable part. Pair them with someone confident.
**Safety and late nights.** Plan B matters most at night. Talk about safe waiting spots, and who to call.
**Apps change.** If the PTV app or Google Maps is blocked, use printed maps; the skills transfer.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It's practical and social, and the free Youth myki makes it immediately useful.

levels.extend: Adds replacement bus and paraphrase to the vocabulary, a quiz question on maps as diagrams, directions for a visitor with specific needs, and Level Ups comparing apps with paper maps and summarising an alert.
